texts: Air temperature
Air temperature: How warm the air is 2 metres above the ground, averaged over day and night.
how warm or cold the weather feels outdoors
mild or chilly weather
warm days and warm years
the climate heating up
balmy or bitterly cold weather
Hottest temperature of the month
Hottest temperature of the month: The highest air temperature reached during each month.
the hottest afternoons of the year
extreme heat and very hot days
scorching summer heat
Coldest temperature of the month
Coldest temperature of the month: The lowest air temperature reached during each month.
the coldest nights and early mornings
frosty mornings and freezing nights
how cold it gets at night
Surface temperature
Surface temperature: How warm the ground or the sea surface itself is (its 'skin').
how hot the ground or the sea surface gets
the temperature of the ocean surface
warm seawater
Air temperature (AIRS satellite)
Air temperature (AIRS satellite): How warm the air is just above the ground, measured from space by the AIRS instrument (average of its day and night passes).
air temperature measured by the AIRS instrument on a satellite
Land surface temperature (MODIS)
Land surface temperature (MODIS): How warm the land surface itself is, seen from space by MODIS (average of day and night). Land only.
how hot the land surface gets as seen by satellite
hot pavement and baking ground
Rain and snowfall
Rain and snowfall: How much rain and snow fall each day on average.
how much rain and snow falls
wet weather and showers
rainy seasons and dry spells
heavy storms bringing water
heavy downpours and torrential rain
light drizzle
Evaporation from land
Evaporation from land: How much water moves from the ground and plants into the air each day. Land only.
water evaporating from soil and plants into the air
plants giving off water vapour
Relative humidity
Relative humidity: How close the air is to holding all the water vapour it can (100% = saturated).
how damp or sticky the air feels
humid and muggy weather
sweaty air
Water vapour in the air
Water vapour in the air: Grams of water vapour in each kilogram of air near the ground.
how much water vapour is in the air
moist air
Water in the whole air column
Water in the whole air column: If all the water vapour above you fell as rain at once, how deep the layer would be.
the total water vapour in the atmosphere above a place
Rainfall (GPM satellites)
Rainfall (GPM satellites): How much rain and snow fall each day on average, measured by the GPM satellite constellation.
rainfall measured by satellites
Evaporation (GLDAS)
Evaporation (GLDAS): How much water moves from the ground and plants into the air each day, from NASA's GLDAS land model. Land only.
evaporation from the land calculated by the GLDAS land model
Runoff (GLDAS)
Runoff (GLDAS): Water that drains off the land into streams and rivers, over the surface and underground, from NASA's GLDAS land model. Land only.
water flowing off the land into streams and rivers
rainwater running off hillsides
Surface soil wetness
Surface soil wetness: How wet the top 5 cm of soil is: 0% is completely dry, 100% is fully soaked.
how wet or dry the very top of the soil is
dry dusty dirt at the surface
Root-zone soil wetness
Root-zone soil wetness: How wet the soil is where plant roots grow (top metre): 0% dry, 100% soaked. Land only.
how much water the soil holds for plant roots and crops
dry or wet fields
parched farmland
Snow depth
Snow depth: How deep the snow lying on the ground is. Land only.
how deep the snow on the ground is
snow-covered mountains
snowstorms and blizzards leaving snow
Root-zone soil moisture (GLDAS)
Root-zone soil moisture (GLDAS): How much water the soil holds where plant roots grow, in kilograms per square metre (= millimetres of water), from NASA's GLDAS land model. Land only.
water stored in the soil
from the GLDAS land model
Vegetation greenness (MODIS)
Vegetation greenness (MODIS): How green and leafy the land looks from space (NDVI): near 0 is bare ground, above 0.6 is dense green vegetation. Land only.
how green and healthy the plants and forests look from space
lush vegetation or bare brown land
plants and forests growing back or dying off
Wind speed
Wind speed: How fast the air moves 10 metres above the ground.
how strong the wind blows
windy and gusty weather
calm or stormy winds
Air pressure
Air pressure: The weight of the air above pressing on the surface.
the weight of the air pressing down
barometer readings
Ozone layer
Ozone layer: The total amount of ozone above you, in Dobson units. Ozone high up shields life from UV light.
the ozone layer high in the sky that protects us from the sun's ultraviolet rays
Haze and dust in the air
Haze and dust in the air: How much tiny particles (dust, smoke, pollution) dim the sunlight. 0 is perfectly clear air; above 0.4 is hazy.
dust
smoke and haze making the air murky
polluted dirty air from fires and dust storms
smoggy air that is hard to breathe
Nitrogen dioxide (OMI)
Nitrogen dioxide (OMI): How much nitrogen dioxide (NO₂, a gas mostly from traffic, power plants and fires) is in the lower air, measured from space by OMI. Higher means more polluted.
nitrogen dioxide gas from car exhaust
traffic
power plants and factories
Sunlight reaching the ground
Sunlight reaching the ground: The energy of the sunlight that arrives at the surface each day, clouds included.
how much sunshine reaches the ground
bright sunny days or dim cloudy ones
Cloud cover
Cloud cover: The share of the sky covered by clouds.
how much of the sky is covered by clouds
grey overcast days or clear skies
Sea level
Sea level: How high the sea surface stands compared with its long-term average, measured from space by radar altimeters. Rising values mean the sea is getting higher.
the ocean rising onto the coast
higher seas flooding beaches and coastal towns
how high the sea stands
Sea ice cover
Sea ice cover: The share of the sea surface that is covered by floating ice. 100% means fully frozen over, 0% means open water.
floating ice on the polar oceans melting
the frozen sea shrinking in the Arctic
ice-covered water
Snow cover
Snow cover: The share of the land that is covered by snow, averaged over the month. 100% means completely snow-covered.
how much of the ground is white with snow
snow-covered land
bare ground where snow used to lie
Snowfall
Snowfall: How much snow falls on land, counted as the water it holds (melted). It doesn't include rain.
how much snow falls from the sky
snowstorms and blizzards
winters with little snowfall
Frost days
Frost days: The number of days in the month when the air temperature dropped below 0 °C.
how many days it freezes
fewer days with frost
a longer frost-free season for farmers
Ice-sheet meltwater runoff

Ice-sheet meltwater runoff: How much meltwater (and rain) runs off land that is covered by glaciers or ice sheets, such as Greenland and the edge of Antarctica. More runoff means the ice surface is melting more.
glaciers and ice sheets melting
meltwater pouring off the Greenland ice
ice caps shrinking
Soil temperature
Soil temperature: How warm the top 10 cm of the soil is.
how warm the soil is for seeds and roots
the earth just below the surface warming up
Deep soil temperature

Deep soil temperature: How warm the ground is about 1.5 to 3 metres down. It changes slowly, so it shows lasting warming or cooling; in the far north it tells whether frozen ground (permafrost) is warming.
permanently frozen ground thawing
the deep ground warming in Siberia and Alaska
Deep soil wetness
Deep soil wetness: How wet the whole soil column is, from the surface down to the bedrock (0% = completely dry, 100% = soaked). It reacts slowly, so it shows long dry or wet spells.
water held deep in the ground
the whole depth of soil drying out over years
Water stored on land (GLDAS)

Water stored on land (GLDAS): All the water held on and in the land added together: soil moisture, snow, water on plants and shallow groundwater, as a depth of water in millimetres. This is a model's estimate from weather data, not a direct measurement.
water stored underground and in the soil
the land's water reserves running low
groundwater and soil water together
Surface brightness (albedo)

Surface brightness (albedo): The share of sunlight that the surface reflects back. Fresh snow and ice reflect most of it (80% or more), forests and oceans very little (under 15%). A falling value means a darker surface that takes up more heat.
snow and ice reflecting sunlight
the ground getting darker as snow disappears
bright deserts and dark forests
Day–night temperature range
Day–night temperature range: The difference between the day's highest and lowest air temperature, averaged over the month. Deserts have a big range, humid and cloudy places a small one.
how much it cools down at night compared with the day
hot days followed by cold nights
Cooling need (degree days)
Cooling need (degree days): A measure of how much air conditioning buildings need: for every day warmer than 18.3 °C, the degrees above it are added up over the month.
how much air conditioning a city needs
hotter summers raising electricity use for cooling
Heating need (degree days)
Heating need (degree days): A measure of how much heating buildings need: for every day colder than 18.3 °C, the degrees below it are added up over the month.
how much heating homes need in winter
milder winters lowering heating bills
Dew point
Dew point: The temperature to which the air must cool for dew (or frost) to form. A higher dew point means more water vapour in the air, which is what makes hot weather feel sticky.
sticky sweaty air on hot days
morning dew on the grass
how muggy it feels
Tropopause temperature
Tropopause temperature: The temperature at the top of the weather layer (the tropopause), 8 to 17 km up, where the lower air ends and the stratosphere begins. It is the coldest level planes fly near.
how cold it is high up where jets fly
the temperature at the top of the weather layer
Tropopause pressure (height of the weather layer)

Tropopause pressure (height of the weather layer): The air pressure at the top of the weather layer (the tropopause). Lower pressure means the top is HIGHER up: a falling value shows the weather layer is getting deeper, which warming of the lower air is expected to do.
how high up the weather reaches
the layer of air with clouds and storms getting deeper
Stratosphere temperature (AIRS)

Stratosphere temperature (AIRS): The air temperature about 20 km up, in the stratosphere (at the 50 hPa pressure level), measured from space by AIRS. While the lower air warms, this layer is expected to cool: the same process with the opposite sign.
the temperature high above the clouds in the stratosphere
the upper atmosphere cooling while the ground warms
Peak wind of the month
Peak wind of the month: The highest wind speed reached during the month, 10 metres above the ground (hourly averages over a wide area, so single gusts are stronger).
how hard the wind blows in the worst storm of the month
gales and wind storms on the coast
Desert dust in the air

Desert dust in the air: How much desert dust hangs in the whole column of air, measured by how much it dims light (aerosol optical depth). Highest over and downwind of deserts such as the Sahara and the Gobi. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
dust storms blowing off the desert
sand and dust carried by the wind from the Sahara
Smoke and soot in the air

Smoke and soot in the air: How much smoke and soot (carbon particles from wildfires, burning fields, engines and chimneys) hangs in the whole column of air, measured by how much it dims light. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
smoke from wildfires and burning forests
sooty air from fires and engines
Sulfate haze in the air

Sulfate haze in the air: How much sulfate haze (tiny particles formed from the sulfur in coal and oil smoke, and from volcanoes) hangs in the whole column of air, measured by how much it dims light. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
haze from coal power plants and heavy industry
sulfur pollution from factories and volcanoes
Methane (AIRS)

Methane (AIRS): How much methane (CH₄, a strong greenhouse gas from wetlands, cattle, rice fields, landfills and gas leaks) is in the air about 7 km up, in parts per billion, measured from space by AIRS.
methane gas from cattle
wetlands and gas leaks
greenhouse gases building up in the air
Carbon monoxide (AIRS)

Carbon monoxide (AIRS): How much carbon monoxide (CO, a gas from fires, engines and stoves) is in the air about 5.5 km up, in parts per billion, measured from space by AIRS. It travels far, so it also shows smoke from distant fires.
carbon monoxide gas from fires and car engines
fumes from burning carried by the wind
Heat radiation from the sky
Heat radiation from the sky: The invisible heat (infrared) radiation that the air and clouds send down to the ground. Warmer, more humid and cloudier air sends more; greenhouse gases raise it.
the greenhouse effect trapping heat
warmth sent down by the air and clouds at night
UV index
UV index: How strong the sun's skin-burning ultraviolet rays are at the ground, averaged over the day (the midday value in weather reports is several times higher).
how fast you get sunburnt
the sun's burning ultraviolet rays reaching the ground
Fine particles (PM2.5)

Fine particles (PM2.5): How much fine particulate matter (PM2.5: particles smaller than 2.5 thousandths of a millimetre, small enough to reach deep into the lungs) is in the air we breathe, in micrograms per cubic metre. The World Health Organization's guideline for the yearly average is 5 µg/m³. Calculated by the MERRA-2 model from its dust, sea salt, soot, organic and sulfate particles; it doesn't include nitrate particles, so city values are on the low side. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
tiny particles in the air we breathe
unhealthy air in cities
air pollution that harms the lungs
Soot (black carbon) at ground level

Soot (black carbon) at ground level: How much soot (black carbon from diesel engines, coal and wood stoves, and fires) is in the air at ground level. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
black soot from diesel engines and chimneys
dark smoke particles in city air
Organic smoke particles at ground level

Organic smoke particles at ground level: How much organic particle matter (from wildfires, burning crops and wood, traffic, and gases given off by plants) is in the air at ground level. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
smoke particles from burning fields and wood stoves
haze from forest fires at ground level
Sulfate particles at ground level

Sulfate particles at ground level: How much sulfate (particles formed from the sulfur dioxide of coal and oil burning, ships and volcanoes) is in the air at ground level, counted with the ammonium that usually comes with it. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
particles from coal power plants in the air we breathe
sulfur pollution at street level
Fine dust at ground level

Fine dust at ground level: How much fine mineral dust (the PM2.5 part of desert and soil dust) is in the air at ground level. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
fine desert dust in the air people breathe
dusty air in dry cities
Sulfur dioxide at ground level (MERRA-2)

Sulfur dioxide at ground level (MERRA-2): How much sulfur dioxide gas (SO₂, mostly from burning coal and oil, metal smelters, ships and volcanoes) is in the air at ground level. The model calculates it from emission inventories (lists of known sources), not from measurements of SO₂ itself, so it shows how known emissions changed. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
sulfur dioxide gas near the ground from power plants and smelters
Carbon monoxide at ground level (MERRA-2)

Carbon monoxide at ground level (MERRA-2): How much carbon monoxide (CO, a poisonous gas from engines, stoves, industry and fires) is in the air at ground level, in parts per billion. The model calculates it from emission inventories (lists of known sources), not from measurements of CO itself.
carbon monoxide from car exhausts and stoves in the air at street level
Sulfur dioxide (OMI satellite)

Sulfur dioxide (OMI satellite): How much sulfur dioxide (SO₂, from coal power plants, metal smelters, oil fields and volcanoes) is in the lowest part of the air, measured from space by OMI, in Dobson units. Daily maps are averaged by month.
sulfur dioxide gas from coal plants and volcanoes seen from space
Formaldehyde (OMI satellite)

Formaldehyde (OMI satellite): How much formaldehyde (HCHO) is in the air column, measured from space by OMI. It forms from gases given off by forests, fires, traffic and industry, so it shows where those gases (volatile organic compounds) are. Daily maps are averaged by month.
formaldehyde gas from forests
fires and factories seen from space
Smoke and dust index (OMI satellite)

Smoke and dust index (OMI satellite): OMI's ultraviolet aerosol index: how much smoke and dust that absorbs sunlight is in the air, seen from space. Values above about 1 mean a lot of smoke or dust; values near 0 or below mean clean air or only bright particles. Daily maps are averaged by month.
smoke and dust clouds seen from space
plumes from fires and dust storms
rivers overflowing and flooding towns
how much water flows down a river
discharge
flood
floods
flooding
how much food farmers harvest
crop production and failed harvests
yield
yields
harvest
harvests
millet
wheat
maize
how full a lake or reservoir is
a lake shrinking or the water level dropping
volume
how cold the wind makes it feel
chill
water evaporating from the surface of a lake or reservoir
